why: Takes no caller-controlled parameters (only ctx); delegates to check_addressbook_access() which runs fixed, constant SQL against the local AddressBook DB with no interpolated argument.
Takes no caller-controlled parameters; get_cached_contacts()/get_addressbook_contacts() (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:439) run fixed constant queries with no interpolated caller input.
Takes no caller-controlled parameters; check_messages_db_access() (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:1747) runs fixed diagnostic queries only.

recipient reaches _check_imessage_availability (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:1498), which never touches AppleScript/subprocess; it is only used to build a parameterized SQL WHERE clause (query_messages_db executes with cursor.execute(query, params), messages.py:206) and the number of '?' placeholders is derived from a caller-independent count of resolved handle rowids, not from the raw string, so no SQL injection surface exists.

name flows into find_contact_by_name (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:608) which only performs in-memory fuzzy string comparison (thefuzz/difflib) against cached AddressBook data; it never reaches SQL, filesystem, or subprocess sinks.

search_term is passed through _escape_like (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:1316-1318, escapes backslash/%/_) and bound as a SQL parameter (query_messages_db(query, params), messages.py:1397); hours/threshold are range-validated (0-87600 and 0.0-1.0) before use. No string formatting of caller input into the SQL text itself.

attachment_id (int, ge=1) is only ever bound as a SQL parameter (WHERE a.ROWID = ?, mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:2364-2367). The filesystem path returned comes entirely from _shape_attachment->_resolve_attachment_path(row.get('filename')) (messages.py:2070-2096), i.e. from the local Messages DB's own filename column, not from any caller-supplied path/string argument, so there is no caller-controlled path-traversal surface through this tool's arguments.
Takes no caller-controlled parameters; server.py:305 runs a fixed literal SELECT with no interpolated input.

hours is range-validated (0..87600, mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:1069-1075); contact/chat_id resolve through find_handles_by_phone/_find_chat_by_identifier which build IN(...) placeholder lists sized from resolved candidate counts and bind all values as SQL parameters (messages.py:1230-1241, 1035-1044); none of the caller strings are concatenated into the SQL text, and no AppleScript/subprocess path is reached by this tool.

start_date/end_date are validated via datetime.strptime with a fixed format (mac_messages_mcp/messages.py:2204-2219, ValueError caught and rejected); contact resolves through the same parameterized handle-lookup helpers as other tools; mime_type is bound as a SQL LIKE parameter (messages.py:2221-2225) rather than concatenated into the query text -- a caller supplying '%' only broadens their own intended filter, it does not escape the parameter boundary. limit is bound as a SQL parameter and validated >0.

excerpt: This server does not perform human confirmation. A boolean tool argument is not human approval (an agent can set it). The MCP client must gate this privileged side-effect before calling the tool.
sink: send_message()->_send_message_to_recipient()/_send_message_direct() (messages.py:661,892,1610) executes an AppleScript `send` unconditionally as soon as the tool function is called -- there is no confirmation flag, allow-list, rate limit, or any other in-code gate between the arguments and the external side effect of actually sending a message via Messages.app.
why: The AppleScript string-injection surface itself is effectively guarded (escape_applescript, messages.py:59-79, escapes backslash/quote/CR/LF/tab/U+2028/U+2029 in the correct order, and is covered by dedicated injection tests in tests/test_messages.py). The remaining gap is structural: the tool's own docstring explicitly admits the server performs zero human-confirmation check and defers all gating to the calling MCP client, and grep of send_message()/_send_message_to_recipient()/_send_message_direct()/_send_message_sms() confirms there is truly no such check anywhere in the code path -- any caller (including an LLM acting on attacker-influenced context) can cause an irreversible, real-world message send with no server-side control. This exceeds what a reasonable caller would expect from a tool advertised as having 'an external side effect' with a stated gating requirement, so it is filed as Tier B (mechanism is real and the advertised purpose itself is to send messages, but the total absence of any authorization/confirmation check on a destructive/irreversible external action goes beyond bare purpose-fulfillment) rather than Tier A, since the risk is contingent on the calling client/agent's own behavior, which this repo cannot control.
contract: This server does not perform human confirmation... The MCP client must gate this privileged side-effect before calling the tool.
